{{DISPLAYTITLE:Programs and proofs in one language}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/The compiler and runtime|Lean theorem prover/System/Monads and do-notation|Lean theorem prover/System/Syntax extension and hygienic macros}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean is a programming language as well as a proof checker. A definition written in Lean can be run
as a program and reasoned about in a theorem, and it is written once for both. This page shows
that, says how Lean turns definitions into programs, marks the places where running and proving
part company, and says how the project this wiki records relies on the property.

== One definition, two uses ==

Here is a definition of the sum of the numbers from 1 to <code>n</code>, a command that runs it,
and a theorem about it:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def sumTo : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => sumTo n + (n + 1)

#eval sumTo 100

theorem sumTo_formula (n : Nat) : 2 * sumTo n = n * (n + 1) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => grind [sumTo]
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints <code>5050</code> and accepts the theorem. The two uses answer different
questions. Running the definition gives the answer for one number at a time; however many numbers
are tried, some remain untried. The theorem covers every natural number at once, by induction
(see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Induction, as the machine sees it|induction, as the machine sees it]]).
Because both rest on the same definition, there is no second copy that could drift from the first:
the program that is run is the object the theorem is about.

== From definition to program ==

Lean runs definitions in one of two ways. An interpreter can run them directly. Or Lean can
compile them: Lean's compiler translates them into C,
one C file for each Lean source file, and a C compiler that ships with Lean turns that into native
code for the machine.<ref name="refelab">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Elaboration and Compilation". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
The paper that introduced Lean 4 describes it as an efficient functional programming language, and
names one reason efficiency matters: people write their own proof automation in Lean, and that
automation has to be fast.<ref name="lean4">Leonardo de Moura and Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language (System Description)", in ''Automated Deduction – CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635. [https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37]</ref>

Lean 4 is itself largely a Lean program. The same paper describes it as a reimplementation of the
Lean theorem prover in Lean, in which users can extend the parser, the elaborator, the tactics and
the code generator from Lean.<ref name="lean4" /> The Lean kernel is the exception: it is written
in C++.<ref name="refelab" /> So the tools that help a person write proofs are Lean programs,
while the part that judges them is kept separate (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/The small trusted core|the small trusted core]]).

There is a free book on using Lean as a programming language, ''Functional Programming in Lean'';
the code in its current edition was tested with Lean 4.33.0.<ref name="fpil">David Thrane Christiansen, ''Functional Programming in Lean''. [https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/ lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

== Programs that act on the world ==

A program has to read input and print output. A proof does neither. Lean keeps the two apart by
type: an action such as printing a line has a type of its own, <code>IO</code>, and a sequence of
actions is written in a block that begins with <code>do</code> (see
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Monads and do-notation|monads and do-notation]]). Continuing the
same file:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def main : IO Unit := do
  for n in [10, 100, 1000] do
    IO.println s!"the sum up to {n} is {sumTo n}"

#eval main
</pre>

Lean prints:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
the sum up to 10 is 55
the sum up to 100 is 5050
the sum up to 1000 is 500500
</pre>

The action <code>main</code> uses <code>sumTo</code>, and the theorem above is about that same
function; to believe it of the values printed is also to trust the compiler that turned
<code>sumTo</code> into a program.<ref name="tcl4">''Type Checking in Lean 4'', online book, chapter "Trust". [https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/trust/trust.html ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
The part that talks to the world is thin; the part that computes is the part that is proved.

== Where running and proving part ==

'''Programs that may never stop.''' Lean's logic needs every function to give an answer, so a
definition that calls itself has to be shown to finish (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Functions that always finish|functions that always finish]]).
A program does not always come with such a proof. Here is one for which nobody has one: starting
from a number, halve it if it is even, otherwise triple it and add one, and count the steps until
it reaches 1. Whether this ends for every starting number is a famous open question, the Collatz
problem. Lean accepts the program if it is marked <code>partial</code>:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
partial def collatz (n : Nat) (steps : Nat := 0) : Nat :=
  if n ≤ 1 then steps
  else if n % 2 == 0 then collatz (n / 2) (steps + 1)
  else collatz (3 * n + 1) (steps + 1)

#eval collatz 27
</pre>

It runs, and prints <code>111</code>. But the program says nothing to the logic. Lean's reference
states that the Lean kernel treats a function marked <code>partial</code> as an opaque constant,
which it neither unfolds nor computes with; all that soundness requires is that its result type
has at least one value.<ref name="recdefs">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Recursive Definitions". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
Even the plainest fact about it cannot be proved by looking inside:

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : collatz 1 = 0 := by
  unfold collatz
  rfl
</pre>

Lean refuses, with the message "Tactic `unfold` failed to unfold `collatz` in", followed by the
goal <code>collatz 1 = 0</code>.

'''Programs run in place of definitions.''' Lean lets a library say that, when a definition is
run, another function should be run instead, usually a faster one. The theorems are about the
definition; the program runs the replacement. If the two disagree, the program and the proofs no
longer describe the same thing.<ref name="recdefs" /> [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What has to be trusted|What has to be trusted]]
shows this happening, and what it costs when a proof relies on the compiled program.

'''New notation.''' Lean's syntax can be extended from Lean, through a system of macros designed so
that names introduced by a macro cannot collide with names in the surrounding text.<ref name="lean4" />
This serves programmers and mathematicians alike, and it is one more thing a reader has to know
when reading a statement (see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]]).

== The project this wiki records ==

Principia Machina depends on this property. Its earlier version kept its rules in prose and
computed them in two hand-written copies, one for the wiki's server and one for the agents that
do research, held in agreement by a large set of test cases. The new version writes the rules once,
as Lean definitions and theorems, and compiles the same sources into one program, the Calculator,
which is to compute every value the specification defines, on the server and beside each agent.
As of 14 October 2026 a first Calculator exists. A test has shown that a compiled Lean program runs
on the wiki's server when started as a command, though not inside a web request, so the server's gatekeeper, Custos, is to call the Calculator outside the web request.
These are the project's own statements, on [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]];
[[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Principia Machina|Principia Machina]] describes the project in
this edition.
